native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB: Individuals with a criminal record (ever jailed 1985-1994) had significantly lower composite wealth than those never jailed in 1985, 1990 and 1996, but the years differ in meaning: the 1985 gap is pre-existing/concurrent and consistent with selection, while 1990 and 1996 are post-exposure gaps. Among NLSY-79 respondents (n=12,013; 289 ever-jailed vs 11,724 never-jailed) wealth was significantly lower for the ever-jailed every year (one-sided tie-corrected Mann-Whitney U, Holm-adjusted p=8.0e-11, 1.2e-34, 9.3e-26; Cliff's delta -0.22, -0.42, -0.35; Hodges-Lehmann shift -$1,260, -$7,850, -$6,000), and the gap widened after exposure (jailed mean wealth 31.6% -> 22.1% -> 19.3% of non-jailed mean; P(wealth>0) ratio 0.81 -> 0.61 -> 0.62). The 1985 difference is not an incarceration effect because jail was measured over 1985-1994, so it largely reflects pre-existing disadvantage; the association is robust to deduplication, winsorization and race x sex stratification but remains observational and unadjusted, so no causal effect of incarceration on wealth is established.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspected file: 12,013x6, zero missing values, ever_jailed in {0,1}, wealth heavy-tailed (skew 6.3-16.6), 24-54% exact zeros, real negatives (min -866,400). 2) Primary per-year contrast, all rows retained, one-sided tie-corrected Mann-Whitney U (H1: jailed < non-jailed), Holm-Bonferroni across the three years within each test family at alpha=0.05. 3) Effect sizes: exact Hodges-Lehmann shift (binary search over 3.39M pairwise differences) with Hollander-Wolfe rank CI and 2,000x stratified percentile bootstrap; Cliff's delta with tie-corrected asymptotic and bootstrap CIs; median and mean differences; P(wealth>0) risk ratio with log-scale CI. 4) Robustness/secondary: Welch one-sided t on raw dollars (anti-conservative, criterion c3 only), Fisher exact on the extensive margin. 5) Cross-checks: 20,000-permutation MWU null, tie-corrected vs uncorrected variance, validation against scipy.mannwhitneyu, and a 300-replication label-permutation negative control (rejection rates 0.033-0.057 vs nominal 0.05). 6) Sensitivities: deduplicated data, winsorization at pooled p99, race x sex stratification (18 cells) with Holm. 7) Applied the approved decision rule per year (Holm-MWU p<0.05 AND median/HL/delta all negative AND Welch p<0.05). Dropped the shifted-log variant because a valid shift must exceed $866,400, which flattens all signal.

sub_hypo.context: NLSY-79 respondents (n=12,013; 289 jailed during 1985–1994 and 11,724 never jailed during that period); 1985 wealth.
sub_hypo.relations: Ever-jailed wealth was significantly lower (one-sided tie-corrected Mann–Whitney U, Holm-adjusted p=8.0e-11; Cliff's delta=-0.22; Hodges–Lehmann shift=-$1,260). sub_hypo.text: Ever-jailed respondents had significantly lower composite wealth in 1990 and 1996 than never-jailed respondents, described in the hypothesis as post-exposure gaps.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY-79 respondents (n=12,013; 289 jailed during 1985–1994 and 11,724 never jailed during that period); 1990 and 1996 wealth.
sub_hypo.relations: Ever-jailed wealth was significantly lower in 1990 and 1996 (one-sided tie-corrected Mann–Whitney U, Holm-adjusted p=1.2e-34 and 9.3e-26; Cliff's delta=-0.42 and -0.35; Hodges–Lehmann shifts=-$7,850 and -$6,000, respectively). These are observational, unadjusted associations, not established causal effects.

sub_hypo.text: The relative wealth disadvantage of ever-jailed respondents widened after exposure compared with 1985.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY-79 respondents (n=12,013), comparing ever-jailed during 1985–1994 with never-jailed respondents across wealth measurements in 1985, 1990 and 1996.
sub_hypo.relations: Ever-jailed mean wealth was 31.6%, 22.1% and 19.3% of never-jailed mean wealth in 1985, 1990 and 1996, respectively. The corresponding ratios of P(wealth>0) were 0.81, 0.61 and 0.62, indicating larger relative disadvantages in the later years than in 1985.

sub_hypo.text: The association between ever being jailed and lower wealth in all three years was robust to deduplication, winsorization and race-by-sex stratification, but did not establish causation.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY-79 respondents; sensitivity analyses using deduplicated data, winsorization at the pooled 99th percentile and race-by-sex stratification (18 cells) with Holm adjustment.
sub_hypo.relations: The negative association between ever-jailed status and wealth persisted under the sensitivity analyses, including race-by-sex stratification. The evidence remains observational and unadjusted, so no causal effect of incarceration on wealth is established.
